> Study B: 93 people, one sample each, three contraceptive methods
> (39 injectable, 28 pill, 26 ring). Before we ask any biology questions,
> we check the data is complete and sane.

```{r setup}
library(conflicted)  # make any name clash between packages a loud error
library(tidyverse)
library(here)

# filter() is claimed by both dplyr and base R. We always mean the dplyr one.
conflicts_prefer(dplyr::filter)

source(here("R/count_tables.R"))

d <- read_counts("group_b")
```

## The sample table

One row per person. 93 rows expected.

```{r}
nrow(d$metadata)
d$metadata |> count(arm)
d$metadata |> count(bv)

# Features in the two count tables (rows of each matrix),
# and the samples in each (columns, should match the metadata rows)
c(
  species_features = nrow(d$species),
  gene_features    = nrow(d$genes),
  samples_in_both = ncol(d$species)
)
```

## Do all tables agree on the samples?

Every table is joined by `sample_id`, so a typo there would silently drop a
sample from part of the analysis. We check all four tables contain the same
IDs, in the same order (DESeq2 and friends match columns to rows by position,
not by name — Tuesday's lesson).

```{r}
ids <- list(
  metadata = d$metadata$sample_id,
  species  = colnames(d$species),
  genes    = colnames(d$genes),
  cytokines = d$cytokines$sample_id
)

# Same set of IDs everywhere?
sapply(ids, \(x) setequal(x, ids$metadata))

# Same order too? (this is what the tests above need to be safe)
sapply(ids[-1], \(x) identical(x, ids$metadata))
```

Missing values anywhere in the metadata?

```{r}
d$metadata |> summarise(across(everything(), \(x) sum(is.na(x)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "missing")
```

## Library sizes

How many reads did each sample get, in each count table? A sample with
almost no reads is unreliable; a few very large ones can dominate
Bray-Curtis distances (which is why we ordinate on relative abundance).

```{r}
mic <- d$species   # shorter name for the microbiome count table

libs <- colSums(mic)          # total reads per sample
summary(libs)

# Flag any sample below 10,000 reads.
small <- names(libs)[libs < 10000]
small

# Same check on the gene table (its libraries are ~400x bigger, so the
# threshold scales up: flag anything under 1 million reads).
gene_libs <- colSums(d$genes)
summary(gene_libs)
names(gene_libs)[gene_libs < 1e6]   # should be empty
```

```{r}
lib <- tibble(
  sample_id  = colnames(d$species),
  species_reads = colSums(d$species),
  gene_reads    = colSums(d$genes)
)

lib |>
  pivot_longer(-sample_id, names_to = "table", values_to = "reads") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reads, y = reorder(sample_id, reads), fill = table)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  facet_wrap(~table, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "reads per sample", y = NULL, title = "Library sizes, Study B") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank())
```

The smallest and largest, so we know the range at a glance:

```{r}
lib |> summarise(across(where(is.numeric), list(min = min, median = median, max = max)))
```

## Feature prevalence

How many samples does each species appear in? Species seen in only one or
two samples are mostly noise for a 93-person comparison.

```{r}
prev <- rowSums(d$species > 0)
tibble(prevalence = prev) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = prevalence)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40) +
  labs(x = "number of samples a species appears in", y = "species",
       title = paste(ncol(d$species), "samples,", nrow(d$species), "species"))
sum(prev >= 10)   # species in at least 10 samples
```

## Do the arms already differ in the metadata?

The study was **not randomised** — people chose their method. So the arms
may differ in pH, BV status or STIs before any biology acts. (Study B
records no age column.) We look now so we know what to adjust for later.

```{r}
d$metadata |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_ph  = round(mean(ph, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
            mean_nugent = round(mean(nugent, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
            bv_pos   = sum(bv == "positive"),
            sti_pos  = sum(any_sti == 1, na.rm = TRUE))  # any_sti is coded 1 = yes, 0 = no
```

`any_sti` values, so we know what codes mean "yes":

```{r}
d$metadata |> count(any_sti)
```

## Alpha diversity across the arms (exploratory)

Diversity *within* a sample (alpha diversity): the Shannon index is high
when reads are spread across many species, low when one or two species
dominate (e.g. a healthy *Lactobacillus*-dominated vagina scores near 0).

```{r}
# Shannon index, computed by hand: -sum(p * log(p)) over the species present
shannon <- apply(d$species, 2, \(x) {
  p <- x / sum(x)
  p <- p[p > 0]      # drop the zeros, log(0) is undefined
  -sum(p * log(p))
})

shan <- tibble(sample_id = names(shannon), shannon = shannon) |>
  left_join(d$metadata |> select(sample_id, arm), by = "sample_id")

p_shannon <- shan |>
  ggplot(aes(x = arm, y = shannon, fill = arm)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, size = 1.5, alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(y = "Shannon index", x = NULL,
       title = "Within-sample diversity by contraceptive method") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p_shannon  # print it so it shows in the report

# Save a copy for the group's slides.
dir.create(here("group_project/figures"), showWarnings = FALSE)
ggsave(here("group_project/figures/shannon-by-arm.png"),
       plot = p_shannon, width = 6, height = 4, dpi = 300)
```

```{r}
shan |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(n = n(), median = round(median(shannon), 2), mean = round(mean(shannon), 2))

# Kruskal-Wallis: do the three arms differ? (rank-based test, no normality
# assumption; the workshop's DESeq2 runs come later for per-species tests)
kruskal.test(shannon ~ arm, data = shan)
```

By eye the injectable arm has the highest median and the pill arm the lowest,
but the spread within each arm is far bigger than the gap between them, and
the Kruskal-Wallis test agrees: **no significant difference** (p = 0.47).
The pill arm looks bimodal — some samples are near 0 (*Lactobacillus*-only)
and others spread out, which is why its median (0.9) sits well below its mean.

## Batch

Which sequencing run did each sample go through? If one method sits mostly
in one batch, batch effects could masquerade as method effects.

```{r}
tab <- table(arm = d$metadata$arm, batch = d$metadata$rnaseq_batch)
tab

# Same table as row percentages: each arm should sit ~50/50.
round(100 * prop.table(tab, margin = 1))
```

For comparison, the same check in **Study A** (the probiotic trial, 176
people sampled pre and post): is the time point balanced across batches?
If all "pre" samples went through one sequencer, a batch effect would look
exactly like a "before versus after" effect.

```{r}
meta_a <- read_counts("group_a")$metadata
table(time_point = meta_a$time_point, batch = meta_a$rnaseq_batch)
```

And **Study A at baseline**: do the probiotic and placebo arms already differ
before the intervention (the "pre" visit)? Same caveat as ours — no
randomisation means no guarantee of balance.

```{r}
meta_a |>
  filter(time_point == "pre") |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_age    = round(mean(age), 1),
            mean_ph     = round(mean(ph, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
            mean_nugent = round(mean(nugent, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
            amine_pos   = sum(amine_test == "Positive", na.rm = TRUE))

# Study A has a handful of missing clinical values (note the NA counts):
meta_a |>
  summarise(across(everything(), \(x) sum(is.na(x)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "missing") |>
  filter(missing > 0)
```

## Open questions & next steps

- **DESeq2 size factors:** the smallest nonzero count in the table is 2, so
  the workshop advice to use `poscounts` size factors applies.
- **Feature filtering before the per-species tests:** we lean yes — keep
  species present in at least 10 of 93 samples (62 of 220 qualify, see the
  prevalence histogram above); 30 species appear in exactly one sample and
  cannot support any three-arm comparison. The composition document already
  uses this filter.
- **Alpha diversity follow-up:** the Shannon difference between arms is not
  significant (p = 0.47), so we do not plan to test it further unless the
  BV-adjusted analysis changes the picture.

## Choices made

- We checked library size and prevalence on the **raw** counts, before any
  transform; alternative was to QC after normalising, which hides low-read
  samples.
- We counted a species as "established" if it appears in at least 10 of 93
  samples (~11%); alternative was a minimum read-count rule, which favours
  abundant species over consistently present ones.
- We summarised arms with means; alternative was medians, which resist
  outliers but are harder to compare in a small table.
- We cross-tabulated batch against arm (and Study A's time point) instead of
  assuming balance; alternative was to skip the check and hope the lab
  randomised well.
- **Samples:** kept all 93; minimum library 5,247 reads (sample B006 flagged,
  kept pending the ordination check). Alternative was dropping B006 now.
- **Features:** QC run on all 220 taxa so nothing hides from the checks;
  analysis docs filter to the 62 species in >=10 samples. Alternative was
  filtering before even the QC.
- **Alpha diversity:** Shannon by hand on relative abundance, tested with
  Kruskal-Wallis; alternative was ANOVA on rarefied tables, which throws
  away reads and assumes normality.
